Technical Guide

Virgin vs Filled PTFE: Choosing a Grade

Fillers turn soft, creep-prone PTFE into a material that can carry load and resist wear — but every filler brings trade-offs. Here is how to choose.

Virgin PTFE has outstanding chemical resistance, very low friction and excellent electrical insulation, but it is soft, it creeps under sustained load and it wears quickly in sliding contact. Filled PTFE addresses those weaknesses by blending a reinforcing material into the PTFE powder before moulding. The right choice depends on which property limits your application.

What virgin PTFE offers

Virgin (unfilled) PTFE is made from PTFE resin alone. It is the default choice when:

  • the media is aggressive and you want the broadest possible chemical resistance;
  • the part is an electrical insulator, or must not be conductive;
  • purity matters — for example in food, pharmaceutical or laboratory equipment (ask for compliance documentation for contact applications);
  • loads are low and static, or the PTFE is well confined.

Its weaknesses are mechanical: low compressive strength, cold flow under load and a high wear rate. For a full overview of the base material, see our PTFE properties guide.

How fillers change PTFE

Fillers are inert particles or fibres dispersed through the PTFE. They do not react with it; instead they carry part of the load, resist the material flowing away under pressure and protect the PTFE matrix from wear. The general effects are consistent across filler types, though their size differs:

General trends from published data. The size of each effect depends on the filler type and percentage.
PropertyVirgin PTFEEffect of adding filler
Wear resistancePoor in sliding service under loadGreatly improved — the main reason fillers are used
Creep / cold flowHighestReduced; bronze and carbon grades are among the most stable
Compressive strengthLowestIncreased
Coefficient of frictionLowest (approx. 0.05–0.10 dynamic on steel)Usually slightly higher; graphite and MoS₂ help keep it low
Thermal conductivityLowIncreased, especially with bronze and carbon
Thermal expansionHighReduced, but still well above metals
Electrical insulationExcellentReduced; carbon, graphite and bronze grades are conductive or antistatic
Chemical resistanceResists virtually all industrial chemicalsLimited by the filler — see the watch-outs below
Tensile strength and elongationApprox. 20–35 MPa; 250–400 % elongationGenerally lower — filled grades are stiffer but less ductile
Mating surfaceKind to soft shaftsGlass in particular can be abrasive to soft metals

Glass-filled PTFE

Glass fibre is the most widely used filler. It improves compressive strength and wear resistance and reduces creep while keeping good chemical resistance and electrical insulation. Glass is the usual first choice for stiffer gaskets, valve seats and general-purpose seals. Watch-outs: glass is attacked by hydrofluoric acid and hot strong alkalis, and it can score soft mating surfaces, so it is best run against hardened or hard-faced shafts.

Carbon-filled PTFE

Carbon (often blended with graphite) gives high compressive strength, good wear resistance and better thermal conductivity. It performs well in water, steam and dry gas service, and is gentle on mating surfaces. Carbon grades are conductive or antistatic, so they are not suitable as insulators. Carbon can be attacked by strong oxidising agents.

Bronze-filled PTFE

Bronze gives the best creep and wear resistance and the highest thermal conductivity of the common grades, which helps carry frictional heat away from a sliding contact. This makes it a standard choice for hydraulic piston and rod seals, guide rings and heavily loaded bearings. The trade-off is chemical: bronze is attacked by many acids and by ammonia, and it is electrically conductive. Bronze-filled grades are also noticeably denser than virgin PTFE.

Graphite-filled PTFE

Graphite lowers friction and improves dry-running behaviour. It is less effective than carbon or bronze at stopping creep, but it is a good option for bushes and seals running against softer shafts, where an abrasive filler would cause damage.

MoS₂-modified grades

Molybdenum disulphide (MoS₂) is usually added in small amounts alongside another filler — most often glass or bronze — rather than on its own. It improves surface hardness and dry-running performance and helps keep friction low. It is a fine-tuning additive: choose the main filler first, then consider whether a MoS₂-modified version of it suits your duty.

How to choose a grade

Work through the requirements in order of how hard they are to compromise on:

  1. Chemical compatibility. Rule out any filler that the media attacks. If the media is very aggressive or not fully known, virgin PTFE is the safe starting point. Our chemical resistance guide includes a grade-by-chemical table.
  2. Electrical requirements. If the part must insulate, exclude carbon, graphite and bronze. If static build-up is a problem, a conductive grade may be an advantage.
  3. Load and creep. For sustained compressive load — gasket bolt load, bearing pressure, seal extrusion gaps — move up from virgin to glass, carbon or bronze.
  4. Motion and wear. For sliding or rotating parts, match the filler to the mating surface: carbon or graphite for softer shafts, glass or bronze where the counterface is hard.
  5. Heat. Where frictional heat builds up, bronze and carbon carry it away better than virgin or glass.
  6. Regulatory and purity needs. Food, pharma and laboratory contact parts are usually virgin PTFE; confirm the documentation you need before ordering.
Starting points only — confirm against your full operating conditions.
If your main requirement is…Start by considering
Widest chemical resistance, high purity, electrical insulationVirgin PTFE
A stiffer, more creep-resistant gasket or valve seat in general chemical serviceGlass-filled PTFE
Dry or water-lubricated running, steam, wear resistance with good chemical resistanceCarbon-filled (often with graphite)
Hydraulic seals and guide rings, highest load and creep resistance, heat dissipationBronze-filled PTFE
Lowest friction against softer shaftsGraphite-filled PTFE
Improved dry-running and surface hardness on top of another fillerA MoS₂-modified glass or bronze compound

Common selection mistakes

  • Choosing virgin PTFE for a loaded sliding part because it has the lowest friction. It will often wear or deform long before a filled grade would.
  • Using glass-filled PTFE in hydrofluoric acid or hot caustic, where the filler is attacked even though the PTFE is not.
  • Using bronze-filled PTFE in acidic or ammonia service because it performed well in a hydraulic application.
  • Specifying a conductive grade as an insulator, or forgetting that carbon-filled parts can carry current.
  • Assuming “filled PTFE” is one material. Filler type, percentage and particle form vary between compounds; always state the grade on the drawing or purchase order.

Filler percentages differ between compounds, so properties for “25 % glass-filled PTFE” from two sources will not be identical. Specify the filler and percentage, and ask for the data that applies to the grade you are buying.
